entries.clue: First picnic club I organised for all to access (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a phrase describing openness rather than a single adjective, but a place for all to access is a public one, so the swap holds.

indicatorNotes.First: First asks for the opening letter of the word that follows and leaves the rest of it alone.
indicatorNotes.organised: Organising a thing means putting it into a new arrangement, so the letters named do not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: the opening letter of picnic, which then leads the rest
five letters of fodder, the clue's own pronoun among them

annotation.surface: A picnic club the speaker set up, open to anybody who wants to come along.
annotation.walkthrough: The lone I is the speaker of the sentence dropped into the mix, which reads much more naturally as a Roman one. Picnic is there for its initial and for the summer it puts in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A public park or path is one anybody may use, so a thing for all to access is public.

entries.clue: Sort out a foreign composer (7)

indicatorNotes.foreign: Foreign asks for the word in front of it in another language, and the article a grid reaches for is the French one.

blocks.note: un is French for a
Maurice Ravel, the Frenchman who wrote Bolero

annotation.surface: Getting the affairs of some composer from abroad into order.
annotation.walkthrough: Ravel is French, so the French article standing in front of him is more than a convenience. Ravel and unravel are the odd pair that mean the same thing, the un- doing nothing at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To unravel a knot or a mystery is to sort it out, taking the tangle apart strand by strand.

entries.clue: Unwell in the French town (5)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the word before it inside the one after, which splits open to take it.

blocks.note: le is the French for the, two letters that come apart
somebody unwell is ill

annotation.surface: Feeling poorly while staying in a French town.
annotation.walkthrough: Lille is the big city of French Flanders, close to the Belgian border and the first stop out of the Channel Tunnel. The French article broken in two around a filling is the standard way a clue smuggles one in.
annotation.definitionFit: Lille is a city in northern France, so town names it by the plain category it belongs to.

entries.clue: Nonchalant sort of labourer (6)

blocks.note: unbothered, taking things as they come
a worker taken on by the day rather than kept on the books

annotation.surface: An unhurried sort of workman.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same word in different parts of speech, the adjective first and then the noun the building trade uses. Nothing joins them, which is why the clue reads as one description of a man.
annotation.definitionFit: Casual means relaxed and unconcerned, which is nonchalant; a casual is also the labourer taken on by the day with no settled contract.

entries.clue: Lots go to the centre for aquatic creature (4)

blocks.note: c is the Roman hundred, the letter a clue uses when it wants a large number
the hub is the centre everything runs into, spokes or roads alike

annotation.surface: Crowds heading into town, and a creature that lives in water.
annotation.walkthrough: A hundred stands in for lots all over cryptics, the Roman C doing duty for any big number. The chub is the thickset river fish anglers pull out from under willows, and it takes only four letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The chub is a freshwater fish of British rivers, so aquatic creature names it by the element it lives in.

entries.clue: Smile after tea causes vexation (7)

indicatorNotes.after: After puts the piece in front of it behind the one named next, so the smile is written second.

blocks.note: cha is tea, the word British English took from Chinese and keeps in a cup of cha
a broad smile is a grin

annotation.surface: Somebody grinning over the teacups, and the irritation it sets off.
annotation.walkthrough: Cha for tea is worth learning: it came off the China ships and survives in British slang. Chagrin arrived from French and keeps its flavour, annoyance with embarrassment mixed into it.
annotation.definitionFit: Chagrin is the annoyance of being humiliated or let down, which is vexation in its slightly old-fashioned sense.

entries.clue: Some gunmetal outstanding (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some wants a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, and that part is already spelt out there unbroken.

blocks.note: the run sits inside the single word: gUNMETal

annotation.surface: An order for gunmetal that has still not been delivered.
annotation.walkthrough: Gunmetal is the copper and tin alloy old cannon were cast from, and the grey that takes its name from them. A concealment inside one long word is harder to catch than one straddling a space.
annotation.definitionFit: A need or a demand that is unmet has not been satisfied, so it is still outstanding.

entries.clue: Each girl really vacant (5)

indicatorNotes.vacant: A vacant room has nothing inside it, so the word in front gives up everything but its two ends.

blocks.note: Eve is the three-letter girl a grid keeps closest to hand
the middle of the word is emptied out and the outer pair left standing

annotation.surface: A girl with a thoroughly blank look on her face.
annotation.walkthrough: Vacant is an instruction rather than a description of the girl, and it reaches back to the word immediately before it. Each and every do the same job in a sentence, which is why either can define the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Every and each both single out the members of a group one at a time, so one drops into the other's slot.

entries.clue: Some prang started causing anxiety (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some asks only for a stretch of what comes next, and that stretch is sitting there already in the right order.

blocks.note: the run crosses the space between the words: prANG STarted

annotation.surface: A small crash that has set somebody's nerves going.
annotation.walkthrough: A prang is British slang for a bump in a car, which is what holds the sentence together. Angst came over from German and keeps its brooding flavour, nearer dread than everyday worry.
annotation.definitionFit: Angst is anxiety of the unfocused, gnawing kind, so the plain word for that unease covers it.

entries.clue: Rapidly spreading liquor finally secured in bottle (5)

indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of the word before it, so only its last letter is wanted.
indicatorNotes.secured in: What is secured in something is held inside it, so the letter goes within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a vial is a small glass bottle, the pharmacist's one
the last letter of liquor

annotation.surface: The last of the drink being locked away in a bottle.
annotation.walkthrough: Rapidly spreading is viral in its modern sense, the one that belongs to videos, though the infection had the word first. Bottle and vial are the same object at different sizes, which is what makes the swap fair.
annotation.definitionFit: Something viral passes fast from one person to the next, whether an infection or a clip, which is rapidly spreading.

entries.clue: Travelling labourer, amusing person in South Island (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In drops the piece before it inside the two words that follow, which part company to take it.

blocks.note: s = south, the compass abbreviation
a wag is a joker, the one always ready with a remark
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea between England and Ireland

annotation.surface: A joker somewhere on New Zealand's South Island.
annotation.walkthrough: South Island is New Zealand's and is the wrong island entirely: the one wanted is Man. A swagman is the Australian tramp of Waltzing Matilda, carrying his swag, or bundle, from farm to farm.
annotation.definitionFit: A swagman is the Australian itinerant who walks between stations looking for work with his bundle on his back.

entries.clue: I arrive, flustered, in the Cannes area (7)

indicatorNotes.flustered: Somebody flustered is thrown into confusion, and the letters named go the same way, out of their order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: Turning up in a fluster somewhere near Cannes.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is the clue's own opening words, which is the hardest place to spot it. The Riviera is the Mediterranean coast running from around Cannes east to the Italian border, so any of its resorts can name it.
annotation.definitionFit: Cannes sits on the French Riviera, so naming the resort points at the stretch of coast around it.

entries.clue: Values old local taxes (5)

blocks.note: putting a price on something, the way a surveyor does with a house
the property tax British councils charged householders until the poll tax replaced it in 1990

annotation.surface: Somebody putting a price on the taxes of the past.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves run together as one phrase, which is what hides the join. The rates were charged on the value of your house, so the noun and the verb are the same word for a reason.
annotation.definitionFit: To rate something is to value it, and the rates were the local tax British households paid their council before the council tax.

entries.clue: Beginner taken in by bloody praise (5)

indicatorNotes.taken in by: To be taken in by something is to be swallowed up inside it, so the letter goes within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a bloody scene is a gory one
L is the plate a British learner driver must show until they pass the test

annotation.surface: A novice swallowed up by praise for something blood-soaked.
annotation.walkthrough: The L-plate is why beginner hands over that letter, and it is one of a dozen words that ask for it. Gory and glory are unrelated words that happen to sit a single letter apart, and the clue lives on that accident.
annotation.definitionFit: Glory is the praise and renown an achievement wins, the acclaim itself rather than the deed that earned it.

entries.clue: With more space and more watery eyes, say (7)

indicatorNotes.more: More turns the word it stands in front of into a comparative, so the eyes are wanted at their worst rather than merely bad.
indicatorNotes.say: Say asks for the sound the words in front of it make, not the way they are spelt.

blocks.note: eyes running with rheum are rheumy, and rheumier once the comparative is applied, which is said exactly like the seven letters wanted

annotation.surface: A place offering more space, and streaming eyes into the bargain.
annotation.walkthrough: Rheum is the watery discharge that gathers in the eyes, and the adjective rheumy sits behind rheumatism too. Comparatives of rare adjectives are awkward on the tongue, which is what lets the sound do the work here.
annotation.definitionFit: A roomier flat has more space in it than the one you are comparing it with, so the phrase says just what the word does.

entries.clue: Insert trendy ballad (5)

blocks.note: what is in this season is what is fashionable
a lay is a narrative ballad, the sort a minstrel sang

annotation.surface: Slipping a fashionable ballad in somewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: A lay is a minstrel's song, the word behind Scott's The Lay of the Last Minstrel, and it is the ballad a grid asks for. Inlay is a cabinetmaker's term: ivory or coloured wood set flush into a surface.
annotation.definitionFit: To inlay is to set one material into the surface of another, which is inserting it into that surface.

entries.clue: A produced American picture (7)

blocks.note: the clue's own article, taken as the letter it is
a thing produced is a thing made
US is the usual short form of American

annotation.surface: A film that was made in America.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening article is a letter of the entry rather than joinery, which is the step most solvers read straight past. Amadeus is Milos Forman's 1984 film of Peter Shaffer's play, Salieri telling the story of Mozart.
annotation.definitionFit: Amadeus is the 1984 film about Mozart and his jealous rival, so picture names it in the cinema sense.

entries.clue: First of salmon, make a selection below boat (5)

indicatorNotes.First of: First of asks for the opening letter of the word that follows and nothing more of it.
indicatorNotes.below: In a down entry below means underneath, so the piece it follows is written second, beneath the letter already taken.

blocks.note: the opening letter of salmon
to cull is to pick out selected animals and take them from the herd

annotation.surface: Taking the pick of the salmon from under a boat.
annotation.walkthrough: Cull is selection in the sense of thinning a herd, the word the news uses of deer and badgers. A scull is both the slim racing boat and the oar that drives it, so the bare definition covers either.
annotation.definitionFit: A scull is the light single-rower racing boat, so boat is the plain category, even though the word also names its oar.

entries.clue: It's enjoyable to almost pour mould (6)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost stops just short of the whole word, so its last letter never gets written.

blocks.note: something enjoyable is fun, the noun rather than the adjective
water pouring out gushes, and the final letter is the one that drops

annotation.surface: The enjoyable part of casting is everything right up to pouring into the mould.
annotation.walkthrough: Mould is the caster's hollow form on the surface and the grey fur on old bread in the entry, which is the whole trick of the clue. It's has real work to do: what is wanted is the noun fun, not the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Moulds are the fungi that grow on damp bread and walls, so the definition names the answer's class by one familiar member of it.

entries.clue: Put up beams, noisily (5)

indicatorNotes.noisily: Noisily points at the way a word is said aloud rather than the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: beams of light are rays, and the two words are said alike

annotation.surface: Hoisting the roof beams with a great deal of clatter.
annotation.walkthrough: Beams are timbers on the surface and sunbeams in the sound, which is where the clue turns over. Raise takes an object where rise does not, and it is the transitive one that matches put up.
annotation.definitionFit: To raise a flag, a glass or a roof is to put it up, so the phrasal verb matches in both sense and grammar.

entries.clue: Unusual object may make you inquisitive, not us (5)

indicatorNotes.not: Not strikes out what it names, so those letters are missing from the word in front.

blocks.note: an inquisitive person is curious
the pronoun written out as its two letters, which are the ones to go

annotation.surface: An odd little thing that arouses your curiosity, though not ours.
annotation.walkthrough: The us to take away is the pronoun itself rather than the abbreviation for America, and it is already sitting at the end of the longer word. A curio is a small object kept purely because it is odd.
annotation.definitionFit: A curio is a small article valued for being rare or strange, which is exactly an unusual object.

entries.clue: Page found in the correct order (5)

indicatorNotes.found in: What is found in something is already sitting inside it, so the letters run unbroken through the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run starts inside one word and finishes on the first letter of the next: corRECT Order

annotation.surface: A page filed away in its proper sequence.
annotation.walkthrough: Recto is the right-hand page of an open book, the front face of the leaf, and verso is its back. The concealment hides under a phrase that reads like a filing instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A recto is a page, specifically the right-hand one you see when a book falls open.

entries.clue: A slap-up outing to European city (7)

indicatorNotes.outing: An outing takes a party out and about, and the letters in front of it travel the same way, out of the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters, the hyphen counting for nothing

annotation.surface: A lavish day trip to a city somewhere in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: Slap-up is British for lavish and is almost only ever said of a meal, which is what makes the outing sound worth having. Uppsala is the Swedish cathedral city north of Stockholm, home to Scandinavia's oldest university.
annotation.definitionFit: Uppsala is Sweden's fourth largest city, north of Stockholm, so European city reaches it as one instance of the kind.

entries.clue: Song first sung in tree (5)

indicatorNotes.first: First takes the opening letter of the word it introduces and leaves the rest behind.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts the letter before it inside the word that follows, which opens up to take it.

blocks.note: a palm is a tree
the opening letter of sung

annotation.surface: The first song anybody sang up in a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: First reads as an order of events and is an instruction about letters. The Psalms are the Old Testament's book of hymns, written to be sung rather than spoken, so song is exact rather than approximate.
annotation.definitionFit: A psalm is a sacred song from the Book of Psalms, set down to be sung in worship.

entries.clue: Without being idle, don't start (7)

indicatorNotes.don't start: Telling a word not to start takes away the letter it would have started with.

blocks.note: somebody being idle at work is slacking

annotation.surface: An instruction not to begin anything unless you are idle.
annotation.walkthrough: Without and lacking are both prepositions here: a house without water is a house lacking water. The comma invites you to read the clue as an order, which is not where it splits.
annotation.definitionFit: Lacking and without both introduce the thing that is missing, so either opens the same phrase with no other change.

entries.clue: Helps wild beast (5)

indicatorNotes.wild: Wild means untamed and out of hand, so the letters after it will not stay in the order they came in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: Lending a hand to a savage animal.
annotation.walkthrough: Abet is almost always in harness with aid, and the pairing gives it the flavour of helping with a crime. Three words leave the fodder nowhere to hide, so the only question is which way round the letters go.
annotation.definitionFit: To abet somebody is to help them, generally in wrongdoing, which is the sense aid and abet fixes in place.

entries.clue: Almost certain to include old bitter (4)

indicatorNotes.Almost: Almost stops short of the whole word, so its last letter is never written down.
indicatorNotes.to include: To include a thing is to take it in, so the letter named goes inside the word in front.

blocks.note: somebody certain is sure, and the E is the letter that goes
o = old, the standard short form

annotation.surface: All but guaranteed to have the old bitter on tap.
annotation.walkthrough: Bitter is the beer on a British pub's pumps in the surface and a taste in the entry, which is where the clue turns. Sour and bitter are distinct tastes to a cook and swap freely in ordinary speech.
annotation.definitionFit: Sour and bitter both name a sharp unpleasant taste, and both describe a temper that has turned the same way.

entries.clue: Goes back up twice as hoarding instant snack (6)

indicatorNotes.Goes back up: What goes back is written the other way round, so the short word named is spelt in reverse.
indicatorNotes.twice: Twice asks for two copies of that reversed pair rather than one.
indicatorNotes.hoarding: To hoard a thing is to shut it away, so what comes next sits between the two copies.

blocks.note: the word turned round gives SA, and two copies of it make the outside
a mo is a moment, as in hang on half a mo

annotation.surface: An instant snack going back up twice on an advertising hoarding.
annotation.walkthrough: Hoarding is the billboard a British street calls by that name, and here it is the verb instead. Mo for a moment comes from the same everyday speech, which is where instant gets its two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A samosa is the fried triangular pastry of Indian cooking, eaten in the hand between meals, which is what makes it a snack.
